item.title: When Mental Illness and Spirituality Intersect
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

When Mental Illness and Spirituality Intersect

Personal Perspective: Holding medical and spiritual truths together.

Posted June 21, 2026

Key points
  • Medical and spiritual explanations can coexist in understanding mental health experiences.
  • Spiritual crises may manifest as mental health issues and benefit from both medical and spiritual support.
  • Suffering can drive an intense search for meaning.
Source: Mike Enerio/Unsplash

I’m sitting beside a brown, bald Santa Claus. Sort of. But instead of asking me what I want for Christmas, he’s asking me, “Who are you?”

It’s taken a long time, a plane ride from North America to India, and several psychotic/mystical/kundalini emergency episodes to finally get me sitting beside H. W. Poonja—this chubby, spiritual teacher dressed all in orange based in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh.

The relentless depression and the terrifying, threatening idea that I would always feel this suicidally desperate were what really drove me there. They say necessity is the mother of invention, but I say it’s suffering.

I Don't Care What You Call It

After several beatific spiritual experiences that catapulted me into psychotic episodes, I was eventually hospitalized, prescribed medications, and offered treatment plans and tongue twisters of diagnoses. Doctors told me I had mild temporal lobe epilepsy and rapid-cycling bipolar 1 disorder with generalized anxiety disorder.

The help offered could have been helpful, could have been soothing even, maybe even a relief had I been in a different mindset, given a different perspective, and offered curiosity by healthcare providers—or, more accurately, by the medical system—instead of directives. But I wasn’t.

So, I refused the diagnosis and I refused medication. Instead, I bought an open-ended plane ticket with my then-boyfriend (12 years my senior) and prepared to get enlightened. Prepared isn’t really accurate—yearned, burned, ached to get enlightened is more like it.

Poonjaji—as he was referred to, with ‘ji’ being a sign of respect—was born in 1910, was a teacher of Advaita Vedanta and a student of Ramana Maharshi. Poonja started attracting students first from his home country, India, and then from all over the world. I was one of those from all over the world.

He was kind, giggly, and at times impatient and cranky. He spoke in riddles that made your mind drop. But he also offered clear concepts that changed your perception. Simply sitting beside him, you would be painted with peace.

I wrote to him prior to my trip to India when I was an open-hearted, easily influenced young woman of 26. I saw him as my road to freedom from suffering. Part spiritual bypassing, part earnest search. 100% last resort.

A Personal Reckoning

Severe depression cloaks itself in many guises. I didn’t see my depression as a mental illness. It was an existential crisis. A personal reckoning manifesting physically and psychologically. The question "what does all this—life—mean?" had pin-balled in my head without pause for at least two years. What sparked it, I’m not sure. It’s the chicken-and-egg scenario.

Did life feel meaningless because I was depressed, or was I depressed because life felt meaningless? Either way, one fed the other.

I searched for answers in all forms: the higher power of AA and OA, self-help books, talk therapy, scream therapy, cognitive behavioral therapy, Reiki, psychics, a sugar-free diet, ecstatic dance. But those mosquito-like questions still buzzed in my brain. "What’s the meaning of life? What’s the point of it all?"

B.I. (Before India), in my blue-walled bedroom, my dad and I were once again talking about my struggle to make sense of this world and why we were here (existing on the planet, not in my room). He warned: "People have been asking those questions for millennia and have never found an answer. If you keep asking yourself that, you’ll drive yourself crazy." Uncannily accurate and unfortunately prophetic.

I’d been told by psychiatrists that what I was going through was clinical depression, that a chemical imbalance was at play—the running theory at the time; then it was bipolar disorder.

But I saw it as a spiritual quest to know my true self more consciously. And it was.

Both Can Be True

Over the years, I’ve learned it can be both. For me, it must be both. Because the relative and the transcendental are one. Not one and the same, but instead they make up the whole.

I can hold two truths at once—the medical and the spiritual. One doesn’t cancel out the other.

A spiritual crisis can be an aspect of a mental health issue and can be helped by medical treatments. A mental health issue can be part of a spiritual crisis and helped by spiritual practices and support. Both have required a recovery of my true self and identity. Mental illness and spirituality intersect. Not for everybody. But for me they certainly do.

I continue to grow my awareness and expand my consciousness. Meditate. Learn. The difference, though, is that it’s not driven by pain and questions; now it comes from a place of curiosity and contentment.

© Victoria Maxwell.

item.title: How I Explain Plant Medicine to My Patients
item.description:
Trauma

How I Explain Plant Medicine to My Patients

Can ayahuasca help treat trauma?

Posted June 21, 2026

Key points
  • Our minds seek sure footing; when the ground beneath our feet shifts, we are usually quite perturbed.
  • A Netflix series follows New York Jets quarterback Aaron Rodgers on a spiritual journey using plant medicine.
  • Hinduism and Buddhism can be used to help understand working with plant medicine.

“When all are one and one is all.” ~ Robert Plant, “Stairway to Heaven”

Since the Netflix docuseries Aaron Rodgers: Enigma came out, I have had patients ask me if they should try working with plant medicine to help treat their traumas. And some patients have asked me to help them integrate what they experienced after they have worked with plant medicines such as ayahuasca and ibogaine. If you haven’t seen it, the Netflix series follows New York Jets quarterback Aaron Rodgers on his spiritual journey, including his participation in plant medicine ceremonies in Costa Rica.

The first thing I recommend is to read the Upanishads and literature on Advaita Vedanta. Personally, I recommend Christopher Isherwood's translation of "Shankara’s Crest-Jewel of Discrimination" along with lectures and books by Alan Watts. Although the Hindu tradition is worlds away from Central and South America, the Hindu concept of Brahman helps people understand what they experience when working with plant medicine. Brahman is beyond our minds' conception as well as any language: the word “Brahman” is just a symbol for something ineffable. The best definition I heard of Brahman in graduate school was “that without attributes.”

What Is Maya and How Does It Relate to Human Perception?

In Hinduism as well as Buddhism, everything that we perceive through our five senses and chunk into narratives is “maya” — illusory and ephemeral. However, human consciousness craves certainty and permanence and appears to be incapable of fathoming reality as it might be actually occurring “out there” in the universe. Scottish psychiatrist R.D. Laing controversially posited that people suffering from schizophrenia had the most accurate perceptions of reality, but for a non-schizophrenic to surrender to that amorphous vastness is usually quite overwhelming. Our minds seek sure footing; when the ground beneath our feet shifts, we are usually quite perturbed.

We do not understand the limitations of human consciousness, what it can comprehend and what it cannot, which is the problem with assimilating the effects of plant medicine. For example, it is impossible for you to imagine infinity. You may have in your mind what philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein called a “placeholder,” such as an image you once saw of the cosmos or a skyscraper, but the finite mind cannot conceive the infinite; it is constricted by categories of consciousness such as space, time, causality, etc. But what if those categories don’t exist “out there”? What if they’re simply our creations?

Why Does the Concept of Non-Dualism Help Integrate Plant Medicine Experiences?

The phrase from the Chandogya Upanishad that best describes what I am describing is “Tat tvam asi,” which is often translated as “Thou art that,” “You are that,” “You are G-d,” or “You are the universe.” This is why understanding “non-dualism” (Advaita) helps people integrate the experience of working with plant medicine: the truth under our perceptions is that our “Self” (capital “S,” higher self, Atman) or “soul” is identical and united with supreme reality. Essentially, Atman equals Brahman; however, humans are trapped in maya, what we perceive through our five senses and chunk into narratives. Plant medicine can liberate us, for a short time, from those traps.

Our mind’s inability to comprehend that the concept of an individual self is "maya" and that we are really all interconnected in one infinite matrix is why many people have trouble integrating what they experienced when they return to their quotidian, individual, ego-based existences. In our bodily incarnations, after we experience traumas, our minds create defense mechanisms in order to help preclude future traumas. This is where plant medicine has helped people such as Aaron Rodgers transcend those traumas—because if we can grasp that we play a role in creating the selves that we inhabit, then we can choose to release the defenses that are inhibiting us from living fully.

item.title: What's a 'Maybelatership' in Dating?
item.description:
Mating

What's a 'Maybelatership' in Dating?

This trending term in dating may be a subset or an offshoot of a 'situationship.'

Posted June 21, 2026

Key points
  • A "maybelatership" is a trending subtype of a "situationship," but it may not be very different in reality.
  • The difference is that the term offers ambiguous potential for progressing to commitment someday.
  • The person could be dragging his or her feet deliberately to keep stringing you on or keep options open.
  • If you're not OK with it, push to define the relationship or at least the timeline and establish boundaries.
A maybelatership is when you are romantically involved with someone in some way, but at least one of you doesn't want to define it or establish some kind of commitment just yet. Instead, the desire is to leave it ambiguous until maybe sometime later.
Source: Polina Zimmerman/Pexels

This isn't a call me maybe situation. It's a "maybelatership." And it may be just a subset or an offshoot of a situationship.

What Is a ‘Maybelatership’?

While the term "maybelatership" may seem to be relatively new, trending on social media, and potentially increasing in prevalence, the concept is maybe not so new. A maybelatership is when you are romantically involved with someone in some way, but at least one of you doesn't want to define it or establish some kind of commitment just yet. Instead, the desire is to leave it ambiguous until maybe sometime later.

This may sound like any kind of "situationship," which I have covered previously in this blog. But there may be one potential distinction. Rather than avoiding any "define the relationship" discussions or saying something like "Let's just keep it casual," that doesn't hint at any future changes, the person who wants the maybelatership indicates in some way that there is the potential of a more committed relationship sometime in the future. The person may say something like “I need to focus on my career at this moment,” "I have to deal with other things right now," "I just need to get past this phase in my life," or simply “I’m just not ready at this moment.”

What Is the Reason for a Maybelatership?

These are all variations of deferring the decision. The specific stated reason can range from the completely vague to the, well, much less vague—but still vague. It's not as if the person says that he or she will definitely commit by May 4, when the fruitcake baking competition is over. Instead, the person is not clear about when or how he or she is going to resolve the uncertainties or even misgivings about you.

Of course, the person could already be quite certain that you are not the one for him or her and be simply stringing you along with no real intent to ever enter into a committed relationship with you. Perhaps you are providing some kind of desired companionship, resources, work, or sex. But deep down, that person doesn't view you as significant other material for whatever reason. A maybelatership can be a manipulative way of offering you more of a tiny carrot than a situationship would to keep you hanging on for longer.

On the other hand, the person could be genuinely confused at this moment, still sorting out his or her feelings for you and gathering information. This can legitimately happen when the person is dealing with career instability, an illness, a family issue, or a crisis of confidence. Alternatively, this could also happen when a person is trying to decide between you and others—real or imagined—as significant others and keep his or her options open.

What Are the Risks of a Maybelatership?

A maybelatership may be totally fine for you if you are truly totally cool with it. Practically any romantic arrangement can work as long as both of you are on the same page and no one gets hurt. You've got to be cognizant of time, though, especially when you get older. Time and effort spent with the wrong fit for you may mean less time and effort available for looking for and being with the right fit. It's also very important to be honest with yourself.

That's because problems do arise when you're stuck with an imbalance in desire, interests, or investment—like when one person wants a committed relationship and the other doesn't. During my school days, I was in maybelaterships twice before realizing that maybe I should have known better. Both proved to be "maybeneverships" and ended up causing me grief, frustration, and wasted time, thinking that something, somehow will get the other person to change her mind. In actuality, one of them was actually being strung along herself by her first choice at the same time.

Keeping someone in a maybelatership against their true interests isn't good either. That person may seem amenable at the beginning, but frustration and resentment will eventually build to the point of maybe exploding one day. Your indecisiveness could eventually make the decision for you when that person wises up and no longer sees you as partner material.

What to Do About a Maybelatership?

A maybelatership can leave you confused and frustrated.
Source: Pavel Danilyuk/Pexels

So, if you are in a maybelatership in either direction, be honest with yourself and the other person. If you actually want a committed relationship with the person, consider pushing now for a define-the-relationship (DTR) or at least a define-the-timeline (DTT) talk. Be frank and honest about what you want and ask what he or she wants. If there's a mismatch, figure out what specifically the discrepancy may be.

Don't accept vague answers. A clear response like "I am recovering from losing [fill in specific thing here], so I need [fill in specific amount of time that's much less than a decade] to sort out how I feel" or "We should wait until we live in the same city [on what specific date]" could maybe merit a little more waiting. But maybe not something like "I'm just not ready for a relationship yet and need more time."

If you don't get the answer that you want, then maybe establish clear boundaries until you do, like "no sex for you," "no gifts for you," or even "no me for you." If someone is dragging his or her feet and you're finding it a real drag, make it clear that your time and effort are valuable, too. It may be time to move on elsewhere.

If you are maybelatering someone yourself, be honest about why. Maybe that person will be totally cool with it. But if not, things won't end well. Remember, wasting someone else's time may be wasting yours, too.

There are claims on social media that "maybelaterships" are becoming more the norm these days. If that is the case, it may be because dating apps can make it seem like there are always so many other options out there that maybe you can keep your options open. But the two options that you will never have are reclaiming lost time and knowing exactly what will happen in the future. All you have is the present, so maybe, just maybe, focus on that.

item.title: Don’t Skip Intro: Opening Credits Are More Than You Think
item.description:
Behaviorism

Don’t Skip Intro: Opening Credits Are More Than You Think

Why the opening credits are an easy opportunity for self-growth.

Posted June 21, 2026

Key points
  • The "Skip Intro" feature was designed based off our behavior.
  • Skipping the intro provides an opportunity to slow down and observe the self.
  • Mindfulness is the act of being aware without judgment.

We’re all watching a different show these days. Yet, whether it’s scripted or not, when the opening credits begin, most of us click that little icon at the bottom right of the screen that says: Skip Intro. Maybe we’re eager to get on with the story. Maybe it’s boredom or too much anticipation that makes waiting feel unpleasant. Or maybe we’re bingeing and can’t be bothered to watch titles for a third time in one sitting. Either way, the phenomenon of bypassing the credits is a fairly recent one thanks to Big Tech’s breakout role in showbiz. A recent article in the Economist reported that the trend started when Netflix observed that its viewers were speeding through opening credits, so in the spirit of making customers happy, they added the feature. Now it’s ubiquitous.

But it does come at a cost. As the Economist noted, the intro sets a mood and evokes the show’s themes. It also creates a threshold between our busy lives and the ones washing over us from the screen. Clicking the button deprives us of this experience and an opportunity to slow life’s pace. As a devoted fan of cinema and TV, I find the openers to be just that; however, as someone who has also binged-watched, I get why we skip intro.

As a therapist, the article called attention to the other behaviors I observe in myself and others: the avoidance of an aversive experience, whether that’s boredom, anticipation, or a distraction from other unpleasant emotions we’re either unaware are happening or unopen to engaging with. This is experiential avoidance, the rigid act of stifling, ignoring or withdrawing from events bubbling up inside of us or occurring outside of us.

Of course, skipping a two-minute introduction to a TV show is hardly the same as skipping a social event because of a fear of being judged by others, smoking weed to avoid grieving a loss, or binge-watching Netflix to ward off boredom or loneliness. Yet, by noticing the Skip Intro as a clue of experiential avoidance, we gain a subtle opportunity to practice mindfulness, which is simply awareness without judgment combined with an acceptance that what’s happening is happening without trying to push it away or alter it.

Clients aren’t the only ones who engage in experiential avoidance—clinicians do too because we’re also human: moving towards pleasure and away from discomfort is natural. However, just because it’s inherent doesn’t help us grow or evolve, and the brief intro could be a chance to get one percent better at the skills of tolerance, mindfulness, and restraint. Everything in our world is in constant flux, whether that’s our jobs, our age, or even our hourly mood and energy level. Our wellbeing is in relation to our ability to be open, aware, and engaged with this reality. Our awareness of what’s arising provides the window to be flexible, to adapt, and to ultimately grow.

Consider that for most of us in the West, access to food is easier than it has ever been in the history of humans, so much so that obesity is a problem, not starvation. Our devices are engineered so that a simple click results in a speedy delivery of toilet paper and goods we probably don’t need. Our diminutive role in producing life’s necessities removes our connection to meaning and purpose. In addition to setting a mood, the credits remind us that it takes a small city of people working together to create our shows—no small feat.

We are lucky to be so comfortable, but we have also set ourselves up to reward pushing unpleasant experiences away with a click. However, like trying to push a ball under water in a pool, unpleasantness comes back up. These emotions might be useful—being open to engaging with them mindfully may release new insights and motivation. So, as we can click away our unpleasant emotions and difficulties, we also click away opportunities for growth and meaning.

Hence, it’s good to take a minute to practice slowing things down. Try it yourself. See what it’s like to experience your life whether that’s driving to work in quiet, resisting the urge to check the phone, or in the passive case of watching TV, sitting through the intro. How does it shift your perspective to notice aversion? What arises or dissipates as you observe without judgment? And how does your experience of the show change now that you’re immersed in its world and your own?

item.title: The Word Workout
item.description:
Cognition

The Word Workout

Why talking is the brain exercise you may be missing.

Posted June 21, 2026

Key points
  • Few people are aware that talking is an important brain exercise.
  • Rates of talking are declining.
  • Tweens/teens and those 65-plus both have low talking rates, on average.
Talking is exercise for our brains.
Source: Liliana Drew/Pexels

Unless you’ve been living under a rock, you’ve heard that you should be walking more steps each day. This advice often accompanies various wearable activity trackers, which both identify a step goal and increase the chances that the wearer meets that goal. I’m wishing we could invent another activity tracker for a different beneficial behavior. My tracker wouldn’t be for walking; it would be for talking. Walking and talking have three big commonalities: They both have proven health benefits, there’s a big range in how much people do them, and they have been declining in our modern society. It’s great that walking has its boosters and activity trackers, but talking also needs a PR campaign and a strategy to increase its prevalence.

Talking Is in Decline

Perhaps you’re skeptical that we need to encourage more talking, especially if you have a relative or coworker who never seems to shut up. Yes, there are still plenty of overtalkers in the world, but when we look across the broader population, we get a different story. A large multi-national study of talking rates shows that while college-aged and middle-aged adults talk a decent amount (saying an average of 12,000 to 16,500 words per day, in these two age groups), tween-teens and people 65 and older average only around 9,000 words per day, barely half of the middle-aged talking rates. And this same study suggests that talking is declining for everyone; we’re probably saying about 3,000 fewer words per day now than 10 years ago. That’s a significant drop.

The Hidden Benefits of Talking

While the value of walking for physical health is well known, the benefits of talking have not been part of our conversation about brain health. We’re so in the dark about the positive effects of talking that I wrote a book about talking’s benefits. I wanted everyone to understand that talking is a mental workout that strengthens our brains. Talking improves attention and follow-through on plans, boosts our learning, helps with understanding our emotions, improves our language comprehension, gives us insight about tricky situations, and more.

Professional athletes are explicitly coached to talk to themselves to reap these benefits and improve their performance. You don’t have to be an athlete to get the rewards of talking, but you do have to talk.

Why Talking Rates Vary

Because talking is so beneficial, it’s important to understand why some groups don’t talk very much. For those 65 and older, a huge factor is retirement, which cuts out all the workplace topics and conversation opportunities that used to come with the job. Unless retirees replace their work-talk with new social activities, they’ll be more isolated and talking will decline. Because low rates of talking are linked to dementia, researchers have staged talking interventions to get older adults to talk more, yielding benefits for both seniors’ mood and brain health.

Meanwhile, teens and tweens often express anxiety about talking and avoid it. Yes, they text, which is also brain exercise, but the addition of texting doesn’t fully make up for the large drop in talking and interaction compared to previous generations of young people. Causes of their lower talking likely include reduced practice of social skills during the pandemic, greater reliance on phones for entertainment, wearing headphones that inhibit interaction, and snowplow parents that do the talking for them. There’s a real crisis here: experts declare that there’s a loneliness epidemic for young people, with huge costs for their wellbeing.

Addressing the Talking Gap

Alas there’s no wearable talking gadget to help us change our talking behaviors. Elsewhere, I’ve discussed steps that senior centers and other groups might take to increase older adults’ talking, and for teens/tweens, a combination of skill building and creating more talking spaces. One small but clever idea that helps both ages is the Call a Boomer program installed in old payphones, which allows young people to call a retiree to chat.

The talking decline requires a multi-pronged approach, which includes more awareness of the importance of talking as important brain exercise. I encourage you to think about how you could help yourself or others to talk more. Perhaps you could call your elderly parents, encourage your teen to tell you about something they’re excited about, connect with an old friend you’ve been meaning to catch up with. If you worry that such steps will be awkward or ineffective, know that studies show that conversations turn out to be more enjoyable than we expect. Go ahead, take the leap, one conversation at a time.
